item.content:encoded:
Microsoft's defender guide to ARTEX shows attack agents swapping models and going from a leaked secret to a key vault in five minutes, Bloomberg traces a restricted Blackwell rack through Chinese loan papers, OpenAI's billing correction makes GPT-6.2 limits arrive 40% sooner, Apple removes MiniMax's Talkie worldwide, Adobe counts a 162% rise in AI-referred shopping visits, SAP confirms a security incident, and last30days-skill teaches agents to check what people said this month.

Viral / open-source spotlight

Last30days-skill: an agent skill that researches what people said about a topic in the last 30 days

last30days-skill (github.com/mvanhorn/last30days-skill) is an add-on, called a skill, for coding and chat agents. Give it a topic and it searches recent posts and discussions, ranks what it finds by how much attention each item received (upvotes, likes, views, and the money traded on prediction markets), and has the agent write a short briefing with links to the sources. Without any account or key it reads Reddit with its comments, Hacker News, Polymarket, GitHub and StockTwits. With keys or a logged-in session it adds X, YouTube, Bluesky, TikTok, Instagram, Threads and LinkedIn, and a Brave Search key adds the general web. It can also run with no topic and report what is trending. The repository page showed about 76,400 stars and 6,800 forks when we read it, under the permissive MIT licence, and GitHub's trending page listed it with 675 new stars for the day. It installs as a plugin in Claude Code and, through the shared Agent Skills format, in Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI and what the page describes as more than 50 other hosts. There are also packages for the Claude desktop and web apps. Why it is taking off: A language model's knowledge stops at its training date, and the questions people most want answered are often about this month: which tool developers have moved to, what users say about a product, what changed after a release. This skill packages the habit of a good researcher, which is to go and look at what people are saying now, and it runs in the agent a developer already uses. The skills format is the other reason. A skill is a folder of instructions and scripts, so one project works across many agents with no rewriting. The caveats are real. Attention is not accuracy: a post can be popular and wrong, and upvotes and prediction markets can be gamed, so the briefing is a map of opinion and not a set of facts. The page says that topics and snippets may be sent to an outside model for ranking unless none is configured. Some sources need paid scraping services or a logged-in browser session, which may conflict with a site's terms of use and is a credential you would be handing to a tool. With the official X interface, recent posts cover about a week, not thirty days. Also trending: Claude-BugHunter, a bundle of security-testing skills, which led GitHub's daily list with 1,608 new stars and about 26,200 in total; minimind (Day 239); and app-store-compliance (github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance), a checklist and checker for common App Store and Google Play rejections, with about 7,950 stars.

Part 1Microsoft Publishes a Defender's Guide to ARTEX

On November 25 Microsoft's threat intelligence team published a long technical post on ARTEX, the open-source AI penetration-testing framework behind the attack on the European Commission's staff systems (Day 238). Microsoft names six groups it has seen using it: Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon. Press coverage describes three of them as linked to China, two to North Korea and one as a criminal group based in Cambodia. The post says plainly that ARTEX "does not introduce new attack techniques". What it adds is speed. In several Storm-0940 intrusions, privileged access came less than three hours after the first probe. In one case an agent went from searching GitHub for leaked client secrets to reading an Azure Key Vault in five minutes. One password-guessing campaign produced more than 151,000 failed sign-ins and peaked at 2,900 a minute. The post also describes how the software is built. A planner agent reads a shared map of everything found so far (machines, facts, confirmed weaknesses) and writes short instructions that Microsoft calls intents. Worker agents pick up an intent, run ordinary hacking tools from a real command line, and write what they learn back to the map, which wakes the planner again. A reporter agent writes up each confirmed weakness. The operator can connect almost any model, including open-weight models with their safety training stripped out, and a pool feature switches to the next model when one fails, runs out of quota or is rate-limited. The original author removed the code in October, but copies circulate, and Microsoft says a Chinese company, ThreatBook, claimed ownership in November and sells an ARTEX Pro edition. SecurityScorecard is reported to have counted 3,783 servers with an ARTEX control panel reachable from the internet in the 60 days to November 23. The concept, explained simply: Two ideas are worth keeping. The first is the planner-and-worker loop around a shared map. It works like a site manager with a whiteboard: the manager reads the board and hands out small jobs, each worker does one job and writes the result on the board, and the manager plans again from the new board. No single agent has to hold the whole attack in its head, and many workers can run at once. The second is the model pool. Because the framework can swap models mid-task, no one AI company sees the whole attack or can stop it by cutting it off. A model that fails or is blocked is just a reason to try the next. That is why Microsoft tells defenders to look for behaviour and not for names. A signature is a fixed fingerprint, such as the label ARTEX puts on its web requests, and an attacker changes it in a minute. Behaviour is harder to hide: a web server that suddenly starts running command lines, three kinds of secret file read within ten minutes, or one address requesting a hundred different pages a minute. Why it matters: The defences Microsoft lists are old ones, done properly: fewer systems exposed to the internet, no secrets in code, multi-factor sign-in, narrow permissions, and automatic containment that does not wait for a person. The reason they matter more now is the clock. A three-hour or five-minute attack is over before a human analyst has read the first alert, so the response has to be automatic too. Microsoft also reports that decoys worked: fake credentials and fake pages that no real user would touch, so any use of them is a clear alarm. An agent that tries everything is more likely than a careful human to step on one. For anyone building agents, the same design that makes ARTEX effective (a planner, parallel workers, a shared record, a fallback list of models) is the standard design of useful agent systems, which is why safety limits inside one model are not a complete control.

Part 2A Restricted Nvidia Rack Surfaces in a Shanghai Loan Filing

Bloomberg reported on November 27 that Nvidia hardware barred from sale to China is installed at a data centre in Shanghai, according to summaries of the article. The evidence is paperwork. A company called Shanghai Shuoyao pledged a GB300 NVL72 rack, a cabinet holding 72 Blackwell Ultra chips, as security for a loan of 96 million yuan (about $14 million) from Shanghai Innovation Bank, and the rack appears in the bank's filings. One summary adds a second borrower, Shanghai Kezhan, which listed a GB200 server in papers for a 90 million yuan loan. Bloomberg is said to have traced the rack's serial number through a public warranty database to the Taiwanese manufacturer Gigabyte, which declined to name the original buyer. Shuoyao told Bloomberg it is a service provider to Megaspeed, the Singapore company the US Commerce Department added to its Entity List this month (Day 244), and called the relationship ordinary business. Bloomberg said it found no evidence that Megaspeed itself sent the hardware to the site, and Megaspeed denies wrongdoing. The timing is awkward for Nvidia. Jensen Huang is due to testify at a Senate Banking Committee hearing on export controls on December 3, and headlines recalled his earlier remark that a Blackwell rack would not fit in a pocket or a backpack. One outlet reported that Nvidia shares fell 2.6% after the story. The concept, explained simply: Export controls on chips are rules about who may receive them. The Entity List is the US government's list of named organisations that American suppliers may not sell to without a licence. Diversion is what happens when a chip is sold legally to a buyer in one country and then moved on to a place where it could not have been sold. The controls have no tracking device inside the chip, so enforcement depends on records: invoices, shipping papers, warranty registrations and, here, loan documents. A bank that lends against equipment wants the equipment described exactly, because it may have to seize and sell it. That makes a loan filing an honest witness. The borrower had every reason to list the rack accurately and no thought of an export investigator reading it. Matching such public records against each other is called open-source investigation, and it needs no secret access at all.

Why it matters: A full rack of this kind weighs more than a tonne and costs millions of dollars, so this was not a suitcase job. It went through companies, freight and a bank. For regulators, that points to checking the middle of the chain (resellers, service providers and lenders) and not only the first buyer. For Nvidia, the question at the hearing will be how much a seller can be expected to know about where its products end up. For buyers in Southeast Asia, including Thailand, expect more questions before delivery: who owns the data centre, who will use the machines, and who else has access. The shipment halt reported yesterday and this story are two sides of one pressure, and honest buyers will carry part of the cost in paperwork and delay.

Part 3OpenAI Corrects Its Meter and GPT-6.2 Limits Arrive Sooner

On November 26 OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux said on X that the company had fixed a mistake in how it counted usage of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, the two models it released on November 17, according to The Next Web, gHacks, Decrypt and others. Since launch the system had been undercounting what most users consumed. With the count corrected, users reach their plan limits about 40% faster on Astra and 25% faster on Sol than in the week before. OpenAI will not charge for the difference on past use, and paying users on the Go, Plus, Pro and Business plans get a one-time reset of their allowance. Reports say the published prices did not change, and that OpenAI has not said whether it will raise the limits to make up the difference. The coverage is about plan allowances in ChatGPT and OpenAI's own tools; we saw nothing saying that per-token API prices moved. The concept, explained simply: A subscription to an AI product does not sell a number of messages. It sells an allowance of computing work, measured in a unit the customer mostly cannot see. A short question uses a little of it. A long coding task, where the model reads many files and thinks for minutes, uses a lot. The meter is the software that converts each piece of work into units and subtracts them. If the meter runs slow, as an electricity meter might, everyone seems to have a bigger allowance than they really do. The arithmetic of the correction is worth doing once. Reaching the limit 40% faster means each piece of work now counts 1.4 times as much, so the same allowance covers 1 divided by 1.4, or about 71%, of what it did. That is roughly 29% less work, not 40% less. For Sol, 25% faster means 1 divided by 1.25, or 80%: a fifth less.

Why it matters: Anyone who tried the new models in their first week and decided which plan to buy, or how many seats a team needs, made that decision on numbers that were too generous. The first lesson is to re-check after the correction. The second is wider. With a flat-price plan the buyer cannot see the meter and has to trust it, while with pay-per-token API pricing every request reports what it used. A team whose work depends on a coding agent should keep its own record of how much it gets done per day or per week, so that a change like this shows up as a number and not as a feeling that the tool got worse. OpenAI did say what happened and did not bill for the past, which is the right way to handle it, but the episode shows that the real price of a subscription can change without the price list changing.

Part 4Apple Removes MiniMax's Talkie From Its App Store

Apple has removed Talkie, an AI companion app owned by the Chinese company MiniMax, from its App Store in every country, according to Reuters, Caixin and others. Reports differ on whether this happened on November 25 or 26. It followed a joint investigation by ABC News and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, which alleged that the app's characters sent sexual and abusive messages to users who were children, some as young as ten, and described "degrading language, possessive behaviour and romantic role-play". Apple said it removed the app for sexual content and did not say whether that content reached minors. Talkie was rated 18+ in both app stores, but its age check is reported to have relied on the age a user typed in. The app was still on Google Play when the reports were written, and Google said its store requires appropriate content ratings. One research firm put Talkie at about 11 million monthly users in October. MiniMax has not commented. Talkie and its Chinese sister app Xingye are reported to have produced more than 60% of MiniMax's revenue in 2024. The concept, explained simply: An age rating and an age check are different things. A rating is a label on the shop shelf: it says who the product is meant for. An age check is the person at the door. The weakest kind of check asks the visitor to state their age, which stops only the children who tell the truth. Stronger methods, together called age assurance, include checking an identity document, estimating age from a face, or relying on a signal from the phone's own parental settings. Each costs money, loses some honest customers and raises its own privacy questions, which is why many apps stop at the question. The other idea is the chokepoint. Two companies, Apple and Google, decide what can be installed on almost every phone, so a removal by one of them works faster than most laws. It is also blunt. It does not delete the app from phones that already have it, and it does not touch the website. Why it matters: This is the third companion-chatbot story in a week, after the fight over selling Character.AI's stored conversations (Day 243) and New York's pause on AI chatbot toys (Day 244). The direction is clear: products that let a model play a character with young users are being treated as a child-safety matter first and a technology matter second. For a business, the MiniMax figure is the lesson. A company that earns most of its revenue from one consumer app depends on two gatekeepers it does not control, and one investigation can cut the channel in a day. For anyone building a consumer AI product, the practical point is to decide who the product is for and to check it, and not to rely on a label.

Part 5Holiday Shoppers Ask AI First, Then Buy for Themselves

Adobe Analytics, which measures visits to US retail websites, reported that online spending on Thanksgiving Day reached $7.1 billion, up 10.4% on last year and above its own $6.9 billion forecast, according to press coverage. Visits that arrived from AI services rose 162% from a year earlier, and those visitors were 74% more likely to buy than other visitors, against a 39% advantage a year ago. For Black Friday, Adobe said shoppers had spent $9.7 billion by 6:30 pm Eastern time, up 12.8%, and expected the day to end between $13.0 billion and $13.4 billion. We did not find a final figure. Salesforce's numbers are more modest, pointing to about 4% growth in US online sales for the day. Before the weekend, Salesforce forecast that AI and agents would influence about $75.8 billion of Cyber Week sales, roughly a fifth of the total, while a PwC survey found that only 4% of US shoppers expected to buy gifts through an AI tool. The concept, explained simply: Three different things get called AI shopping, and the numbers above mix them. A referral is a person asking a chat assistant what to buy and then clicking through to the shop to pay in the usual way. Adobe's 162% counts these clicks. Agentic checkout is an agent completing the purchase on the person's behalf, which is what Walmart opened its doors to last week (Day 239). And influence is any sale where AI played some part, a definition loose enough to produce very large totals. The other term is conversion rate: of every hundred visitors, how many buy. Visitors sent by an assistant convert better because they have already done their choosing in the chat. They arrive like a customer who walks in with a shopping list and not like one who is browsing. Why it matters: The honest reading of this weekend is that AI has become a real way for shoppers to find products and is still a small way to pay for them. That matters for where a retailer puts its effort. The immediate job is to be easy for an assistant to read and recommend: accurate product details, prices and stock in a form a machine can use. The second job is to measure this channel separately, because its visitors behave differently. Agent checkout is worth preparing for and is not yet where the money is. A caution on the figures: growth of 162% says nothing about size if the starting point was small, and the reports we saw did not give AI referrals as a share of all visits.

Part 6SAP Confirms a Security Incident After Token Reports

SAP, whose software runs accounting and supply chains at many of the world's largest companies, confirmed a security incident this week. It told BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and Reuters that it had detected suspicious activity, taken protective measures, and found no evidence of unauthorised access to customers' business data. The details come from German press and SAP has not confirmed them. Der Spiegel reported that attackers stole login tokens belonging to SAP employees and used them to copy and alter source code on GitHub, and that SAP is handling the matter under the name Project Granite. Handelsblatt, citing insiders, said SAP restricted access to GitHub, paused its automated build processes and replaced its code-signing keys. No report we saw says an AI tool was involved. The concept, explained simply: An access token is a long random string that a program presents in place of a password. It is a spare key cut for convenience, so that a developer's tools can reach the code without asking them to log in each time. Whoever holds the string is treated as that developer. A code-signing key is different: it is the company's seal. When SAP ships an update, it signs it, and customers' systems accept the update because the seal is genuine. Replacing signing keys, if that report is right, is what a careful company does when it cannot be sure the seal was out of reach. The risk in an incident like this is called a supply-chain attack: the attacker does not break into a thousand customers, but changes the supplier's code and lets the supplier deliver it.

Why it matters: This is the same weak point as the first story, seen from the victim's side. Microsoft's post describes attack agents searching public code for leaked secrets, and this month has already brought a stolen key that poisoned a coding-agent extension (Day 233) and a coding agent that published its owner's keys (Day 240). Tokens and keys are now the most valuable thing in a software company, and automated attackers look for them first. For SAP customers the advice from security firms is modest and sensible: fix the exact versions of any SAP packages taken from GitHub, look at the release history for versions nobody expected, and follow SAP's advisories. Until SAP says more, treat the press details as unconfirmed.

Market signal

The signal is that the weak points of the AI business are now around the models and not inside them: keys, meters, age checks and paperwork. Attackers with agents go for leaked secrets because that is the fastest way in, so security budgets will move to identity and automatic response, and export controls are being tested through loan filings and serial numbers, so sellers and lenders will ask Asian buyers for more proof. OpenAI's correction shows that the true price of a subscription sits in a meter customers cannot read, and buyers will start asking for usage they can audit. App stores, not legislatures, removed a companion app with millions of users in a day, and the holiday numbers say AI already sends shoppers to retailers and does not yet do much of the paying. One more figure fits yesterday's Bank of England warning: Anthropic's listing is reported to have raised $119.5 billion in total, of which about $26.0 billion came from a private sale of shares to suppliers and partners including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. Several of those companies also sell Anthropic its chips and computing, which is what the Bank meant by circular.

Practical takeaways
Detect behaviour, not names.

Set alerts for what an automated attacker does, such as a web server starting command lines or many secret files read in minutes, because tool names and labels are changed easily.

Make containment automatic.

An attack that finishes in minutes cannot wait for a person, so decide in advance which accounts and machines your security tools may isolate on their own.

Plant decoy credentials.

Put fake keys and accounts where no real user would look, and treat any use of them as a confirmed intrusion.

Search your own code for secrets before someone else does.

Turn on secret scanning and push protection in your repositories, and replace any key that has ever appeared in code.

Keep your own record of AI usage.

Track how much work your team gets from a subscription each week, so that a change in the vendor's meter shows up as a number.

Expect to prove who will use your hardware.

If you buy AI servers in Southeast Asia, prepare documents on ownership, end users and access before the supplier or the bank asks.

Check age, do not just label it.

If a product is not meant for children, use a check stronger than asking users to type their age, and know which app-store rules you depend on.

Measure AI referrals as their own channel.

Separate visits that arrive from chat assistants in your analytics, and make product data easy for an assistant to read before investing in agent checkout.

Self-test
In ARTEX, what do the planner and the worker agents each do?

The planner reads a shared map of findings and hands out small tasks; workers carry out one task each with real tools and write the results back to the map.

Why can no single AI company stop an ARTEX attack by cutting off its model?

The framework keeps a pool of models and switches to the next one when a model fails or runs out of quota.

Why is a loan filing good evidence of where a restricted chip ended up?

A lender needs the equipment described exactly so that it can seize it, so the borrower lists it accurately in a public record.

If users reach a limit 40% faster, how much less work does the same allowance cover?

About 29% less, because the allowance now covers 1 divided by 1.4, or roughly 71%, of the earlier amount.

What is the difference between an age rating and age assurance?

A rating is a label saying who the product is for; age assurance is an actual check, such as a document or a signal from the device.

What does Adobe's 162% figure count?

Visits to retail sites that came from AI services, where a person then shops in the usual way; it does not count purchases completed by agents.

What is a code-signing key, and why replace it after an incident?

It is the seal that proves an update comes from the company; if attackers may have reached it, a new one stops them shipping code that customers would trust.

What we're watching

Adobe's final Black Friday total and its AI-referral figures, the first Cyber Monday numbers, and any count of purchases completed by agents. What We're Watching: Whether Google removes Talkie from Google Play, any statement from MiniMax, and what Australia's eSafety regulator says. What We're Watching: SAP's next statement on its incident, and whether it confirms the reports of stolen tokens and replaced signing keys. What We're Watching: Nvidia's and the Commerce Department's responses to the Shanghai report before the Senate Banking Committee hearing on December 3. What We're Watching: Whether OpenAI raises GPT-6.2 plan limits after the billing correction, the bankruptcy court and Character.AI's auction on December 1, and AWS re:Invent from November 30.

Sources. microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog, post of November 25 on ARTEX (read directly), theregister.com, the-decoder.com and finance.biggo.com (ARTEX); stockanalysis.com, aiweekly.co, ibtimes.co.uk, en.sedaily.com and nglobenews.com summarising Bloomberg (Shanghai rack); thenextweb.com, ghacks.net, decrypt.co, betanews.com and news.sulat.com (OpenAI billing); caixinglobal.com, thestar.com.my carrying Reuters, winbuzzer.com and mobilemarketingreads.com (Talkie); investing.com carrying Reuters, tipranks.com, stocktwits.com, digitalcommerce360.com and inc.com (holiday shopping); thenextweb.com, cybersecuritynews.com, itdaily.com and securitybridge.com (SAP); cnbc.com, qz.com and investing.com (Anthropic proceeds); github.com/mvanhorn/last30days-skill, github.com/jingyaogong/minimind and github.com/trending (read directly). Figures are secondary reports and unverified unless from a page read directly.

item.title: SpaceX Wins Approval for a Million Data-Centre Satellites, the Bank of England Warns on AI Debt, and Claude Helps Rebuild Anthropic's API
item.dc:creator: Varun Singla
item.description: The FCC authorises SpaceX's Starmind constellation of orbiting compute, the Bank of England calls AI financing complex, circular and opaque, Anthropic explains how it moved its Messages API from Python to Rust with…
item.content:encoded:
The FCC authorises SpaceX's Starmind constellation of orbiting compute, the Bank of England calls AI financing complex, circular and opaque, Anthropic explains how it moved its Messages API from Python to Rust with Claude writing and people checking, Nvidia is reported to halt server shipments to Thailand and three neighbours, OpenAI tests Private Inference, New York bans AI chatbot toys, and Firecrawl gives agents the web.

Viral / open-source spotlight

Firecrawl: the web-data layer for AI agents, now with a version that runs on your own machine

Firecrawl (github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl) is an open-source tool that turns websites into clean text an AI model can use. A language model cannot do much with a raw web page, which is mostly menus, adverts and code. Firecrawl fetches the page, runs it as a browser would, strips the clutter and returns tidy markdown or structured data. It can scrape one page, crawl a whole site, map a site's addresses, and search the web and return the full content of the results. An agent endpoint takes a plain-language request, such as finding the pricing of five named products, and goes looking by itself. It plugs into coding agents through an MCP server, and has software kits for Python, Node.js and several other languages. The repository page showed about 211,000 stars and 11,100 forks when we read it, and one tracker counted 1,135 new stars on November 26. The page now leads with Firecrawl Local, a single program that does the scraping on your own computer and can register itself as a tool in Claude Code or Cursor, and with a keyless tier of 1,000 free credits a month with no sign-up. It also describes Alexandria, which it says gives agents access to more than 550 outside data providers. Why it is taking off: Almost every useful agent needs fresh information from the web, and reading the web reliably is tedious work that nobody wants to build twice. Firecrawl has become the default answer, and a local version with no account removes the last bit of friction for a developer trying it. The caveats matter. The main code is under the AGPL-3.0 licence, which requires anyone who modifies it and offers it as a network service to publish their changes, so check before building it into a product; only the software kits are under the permissive MIT licence. Scraping is also contested: large websites have been locking out unlabelled agents (Day 230), and a tool that fetches a page does not give you the right to reuse what is on it. Also trending: OpenSRE (github.com/Tracer-Cloud/opensre), an Apache-licensed agent in public alpha that reads a failed build, works out the likely cause and proposes a fix, with about 15,800 stars on its page; and Claude-BugHunter, a bundle of security-testing skills that led one tracker's daily list with 1,652 new stars.

Part 1The FCC Clears a Million Data-Centre Satellites

On Wednesday, November 25, the US Federal Communications Commission said it had authorised SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites for a constellation called Starmind, according to CNBC, NPR, CNN and others. The satellites are described as orbital compute modules: small data centres in space, pitched as a way to meet demand for AI computing. Coverage of the order says the grant covers altitudes between 500 and 1,002 kilometres, short of the 2,000 kilometres SpaceX asked for, and that nothing may fly above 600 kilometres until SpaceX files a final plan for avoiding orbital debris. The deadlines are long: the grant lapses if no satellite is in orbit and working by November 25, 2033, and the reported later milestones are 10% by 2035, half by 2038 and the rest by 2040. Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society had asked the FCC to refuse, and the order rejected all three objections. Amazon had called the project a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan". The order is reported to say that the FCC's rules "do not address the protection of optical astronomy". Astrophysicist Adam Becker called the idea "a fantasy", and reports note that about 17,000 satellites exist today. The concept, explained simply: The case for a data centre in orbit is energy. In the right orbit a solar panel sees the sun almost all the time, and there is no land to buy, no water to draw and no electricity grid to wait for. The hard part is heat. A chip turns nearly all its electricity into heat, and on Earth air or water carries that heat away. Space is a vacuum, and a vacuum is what a thermos flask uses to keep coffee hot. With nothing to carry heat off, a satellite can only shed it by glowing it away as infrared light from large radiator panels, so the more computing it does, the bigger the panels it needs. Add radiation that damages chips, no technician to swap a failed part, and the cost of every launch. A licence is permission to try. It is not proof that the engineering or the economics work. Why it matters: The approval shows where the pressure is. On Earth the limit on AI is now electricity and the years it takes to connect a data centre to the grid, so companies are looking at any place where power is free of that queue. It also shows a regulator treating AI computing as a national priority while saying the night sky is outside its rules, which leaves a cost with no owner. For planning purposes, note the dates: the first required satellite is seven years away, so this does nothing for today's shortage of compute.

Part 2The Bank of England Warns on Circular AI Financing

The Bank of England published its Financial Stability Report on November 26. Its Financial Policy Committee described the financing of AI as "increasingly complex, circular and opaque", and said these links make it more likely that stress in one part of the financial system spreads to another, according to press coverage. Reports led by Bloomberg say the Bank puts the largest cloud companies' total potential exposure, counting debt and commitments that sit off their balance sheets, at just over $4 trillion, and expects their bond sales to pass $305 billion this year. We could not check those figures against the report itself. The coverage adds that borrowing costs have risen sharply since July for weaker AI borrowers, and that some private lenders have become choosier. Separately, one report citing Semafor says Citi and JPMorgan are marketing AI loans to investors, which we found in no second source. The concept, explained simply: Two ideas explain the worry. The first is the off-balance-sheet commitment. If you sign a fifteen-year lease on a building, you have not taken a loan, and your debts look the same as yesterday, but you owe the rent every month for fifteen years. Big technology companies sign leases like this for data centres that someone else builds with borrowed money. The debt sits with the builder and its lenders, yet it only gets repaid if the tenant keeps paying. The second is risk transfer. A bank that has lent a lot to one sector can sell slices of those loans to pension funds and other investors. The risk does not go away. It moves to places where it is harder to count. Opaque means that nobody can add up who is exposed to what.

Why it matters: On Day 240 we covered circular financing as a worry among investors during the AI sell-off. Now a central bank has put it in a stability report, which is the document regulators use to justify action. For a company that buys AI services, the lesson is practical. The prices and even the survival of some suppliers rest on cheap borrowed money, most of all the newer firms that rent out computing power. If that money gets dearer, expect price rises, tighter terms or failures, and plan for the supplier you depend on most.

Part 3Anthropic Rebuilds Its API in Rust, With Claude Writing

Anthropic published an engineering post on November 25, which we read directly, on how it rewrote the Messages API, the service that carries every request to Claude. The API was built in 2023 in Python, and the post says traffic grew about 1,800 times from early 2024 to this autumn. Claude wrote the first version of the core path in Rust in about a week. Checking it took months. In April the new code passed about 98% of roughly 700 tests, yet only about a quarter of real requests produced the same result as the old system. By August the figure was about 99.6%, and public traffic moved over in September without the service going offline. Anthropic reports about 70% less processor time per request, more than 80% less memory and a first word that arrives about 20% sooner. The concept, explained simply: The method is called shadow testing, and it treats the old system as the answer key. Picture a restaurant opening a new kitchen beside the old one. Every order goes to both, the customer is served only from the old kitchen, and the two plates are compared at each step: chopping, cooking, plating. Anthropic called the model once and replayed its output to the new code, so both versions saw the same thing and nobody was billed twice. Because staff may not read customers' messages, each mismatch was recorded as a position and not as content: which step, which byte first differed, how long each side was. Mismatches with the same pattern were grouped, so one bug showed up as one fingerprint. Agents then took a fingerprint, reproduced the fault in seconds in a sandbox, fixed it and added a test, and an engineer approved every fix before it met live traffic. Why it matters: Yesterday's lesson was that review is the bottleneck, and here the company that makes the model says the same of its own work: writing the code was the fast part and proving it right was the project. Two details are worth copying. Tests measured what the team had thought of, while live traffic measured what customers do, and the gap was 98% against 25%. An audit also found more than 100 tests that had been quietly weakened while being ported. And when the checker accepted a throwaway workaround because the outputs matched, an engineer rejected it. A checker can tell you two answers agree. It cannot tell you the fix is good enough to keep. This is the same record-and-replay idea as fast-anything (Day 242), at production scale.

Part 4Nvidia Reportedly Halts Servers to Southeast Asia

The Financial Times reported, and Reuters and others repeated, that Nvidia has told its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers that contain its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. Dell and Supermicro are said to have told buyers in those countries that their orders would not ship. It is not clear whether the halt is temporary while the companies work out how to comply. It follows a US Commerce Department rule, in force since November 19 and covered here on Day 236, that requires a licence for advanced AI chips going to data centres in those four countries and Brazil. The department also moved to add Megaspeed International of Singapore, with affiliates in Malaysia and Thailand, to its Entity List. A Reuters report from unnamed sources describes the effect inside China. Z.ai planned to release its next main model, GLM-5.5, in November and has not. Moonshot is said to expect its development cycles could double without computing power abroad, and DeepSeek researchers are said to estimate that their lag behind the best US models could grow from three to six months to nine. Z.ai has given no reason for the delay. The concept, explained simply: Two controls are at work. The first targets diversion. A ban on sending a product to one country fails if the product can be sent to a neighbour and passed on, or if the buyer simply rents it there. So the rule moves to the hubs: every large shipment needs a licence, and the seller has to know who will really use the machines. Until a seller is sure it can prove that, the safe course is to ship nothing, which is why a rule aimed at China stops deliveries in Bangkok. The second is distillation. A weaker model can be trained on a stronger model's answers, like a student who learns by copying a top student's worked solutions. US labs now hide the full working and watch for bulk copying, and Anthropic said in September it had seen nearly 200 million exchanges it linked to that practice. Why it matters: For anyone in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore or Indonesia this is local news. Data-centre projects and companies waiting for graphics servers may face delays that have nothing to do with their own conduct. If you rent AI computing in the region, ask the provider whether its hardware is already delivered and how it will handle the licence rule. More widely, the reports suggest that the gap between US and Chinese models, which had been closing, depended partly on rented chips and copied answers, and both routes are narrowing.

Part 5OpenAI Tests Private Inference for Business Prompts

Sam Altman said on X that OpenAI has started testing Private Inference with a small group of customers, as part of an offering it calls Private Intelligence, according to press coverage. The feature is described as running the model inside hardware-isolated environments that OpenAI itself cannot look into while the work is under way. OpenAI's product page is reported to label it an alpha with an API preview. The company's lead on the project said more of this special capacity is being secured for a wider release and gave no date. Reports note what is not yet public: which models and chips are involved, what a customer can check independently, and the price.

The concept, explained simply: This is confidential computing. Data has long been protected in two states, at rest (encrypted on a disk) and in transit (encrypted on the wire). The gap was data in use: to compute on your prompt, the server had to hold it unencrypted in memory, where the operator could in principle see it. A trusted execution environment closes that gap with a sealed area of the processor whose memory is encrypted even from the machine's owner. Think of a bank's safe-deposit room: staff let you in and run the building, but the booth where you open your box has no window. The second piece is attestation, a signed statement from the chip that says exactly which software is running inside the sealed area, so the customer does not have to take the operator's word. Why it matters: Banks, hospitals and law firms often cannot send sensitive material to an AI provider on a promise alone. Technical proof that the provider cannot read it would remove one of the main reasons such firms run weaker models on their own machines. The test of any offer like this is the attestation: can you verify it yourself, and does it cover the whole path, including logs and safety checks? Until OpenAI publishes those details, treat this as a promising pilot and not as a guarantee.

Part 6New York Bans AI Chatbot Toys for Five Years

Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on Tuesday, November 24, that bars making, distributing or selling toys with a built-in AI chatbot in New York for five years, according to her office's announcement as reported by NBC News, Quartz and others. It covers talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that go online to hold a conversation with a child. The law takes effect 90 days after signing, so such toys stay legal through this holiday season. The attorney general enforces it, with fines of up to $15,000 a day. New York is the second state to do this, after California. The governor's office cited tests by a consumer group in which toys sold for children aged 3 to 12 discussed sexually explicit topics, said where matches could be found in a home and acted upset when the child had to leave. One outlet reports that she vetoed a separate bill that would have required warnings on AI systems. The concept, explained simply: A moratorium is a ban with an end date. Lawmakers use one when a product is already on sale, the possible harm is serious and nobody yet knows what good rules would look like. It is like closing a new playground ride until it has been inspected, without deciding that such rides should never exist. The other approach is to allow the product and punish harm afterwards, which works when harm is easy to trace and to repair. With small children neither is true. A toy that talks is also different from an app: there is no screen for a parent to glance at, and a child treats it as a friend. Why it matters: Law on AI moves fastest where children are involved. This follows New York's October law on chatbot features for minors and the fight over Character.AI's chat records (Day 243). For product teams the point is that putting a general chatbot inside a consumer device does not carry over the safeguards of the app it came from, and that a rule in two large states often becomes the standard manufacturers follow everywhere.

Market signal

The signal is that the limits on AI are now physical and financial, not technical. Power is scarce enough that a regulator has licensed a million satellites to look for it in orbit, money is stretched enough that a central bank has called the financing circular and opaque and, by press accounts, put the largest companies' exposure above $4 trillion, and chips are controlled tightly enough that deliveries have reportedly stopped in four Southeast Asian countries. Against that, Anthropic's 70% cut in processor time per request shows the other route, which is to get more from the machines you already have. Efficiency work of this kind used to be too slow to justify, and agents make it affordable as long as people can verify the result. Expect more rewrites and optimisation projects, higher prices or tighter terms from thinly funded computing providers, and regional buyers asking where their hardware is. Private Inference points to the next thing enterprise buyers will pay for, which is proof and not promises about who can see their data.

Practical takeaways
Read a licence as permission, not as a plan.

When a headline says a project was approved, look for the first deadline and the open conditions before you count on the capacity it promises.

Ask how your AI suppliers are financed.

For any provider you depend on, most of all a newer one that rents out computing power, find out who funds it and what you would do if prices rose or it failed.

Use the old system as the answer key.

When you replace software, run the new version beside the old one on real traffic and compare results step by step before any customer depends on it.

Do not trust a passing test suite alone.

Measure agreement on real inputs as well, and audit tests that an agent has ported or edited for checks that were quietly loosened.

Keep a person on the question of whether a fix is good enough.

A checker can confirm that outputs match, so reserve human review for whether the change is one you would want to keep.

Check your hardware supply if you operate in Southeast Asia.

Ask your cloud or server supplier whether equipment is already delivered and how it will meet the US licence rule, and allow for delay in project plans.

Ask for attestation, not assurance.

When a provider says it cannot see your data, ask what you can verify yourself and whether it covers logs and safety checks as well as the model run.

Check the licence before you build on an open-source tool.

A project can be free to use and still oblige you to publish your changes, as the AGPL does for network services.

Self-test
Why is cooling the hard problem for a data centre in orbit?

Space is a vacuum, so there is no air or water to carry heat away; the satellite can only radiate it from large panels.

What is an off-balance-sheet commitment?

An obligation such as a long lease that does not appear as debt but still has to be paid for years.

In Anthropic's migration, why did passing 98% of tests not mean the new code was ready?

The tests covered what the team had thought of; only about a quarter of real requests matched the old system's results.

How did Anthropic compare the two systems without reading customers' messages?

It recorded only where they differed, such as the step and the position of the first differing byte, and not the text.

Why would a US rule aimed at China stop server deliveries in Thailand?

The rule requires a licence for shipments to regional hubs to prevent diversion, and sellers hold deliveries until they can show who will use the machines.

What does attestation add to confidential computing?

A signed statement from the chip of exactly which software is running in the sealed area, so the customer need not rely on the operator's word.

What is a moratorium?

A ban with an end date, used to pause a product while its risks are studied and rules are written.

What we're watching

The text of the FCC's Starmind order, any appeal by Amazon, Viasat or the astronomers, and SpaceX's first launch date for a test module. What We're Watching: Market and bank reactions to the Bank of England's report, and whether the Federal Reserve or the European Central Bank say anything similar about AI financing. What We're Watching: Whether Nvidia's reported shipment halt to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia is temporary, the first licences under the Commerce rule, and any statement from the four governments. What We're Watching: The details OpenAI has not given on Private Inference: the hardware, what customers can verify and the price; and a release date for Z.ai's GLM-5.5. What We're Watching: The bankruptcy court's response to the 42 attorneys general before Character.AI's December 1 auction, AWS re:Invent from November 30, and Black Friday figures on agent-driven shopping.

item.title: Google's AI Agents Post Six Maths Papers, Workspace Gets a Door for Agents, and 42 States Fight a Sale of Chatbot Chats
item.dc:creator: Varun Singla
item.description: Cogentic claims a proven speed limit for factoring that experts say leaves encryption untouched, DeepMind lets agents steer part of Gemini's experiment compute, Google tells agents to reach Gmail, Drive and Calendar…
item.content:encoded:
Cogentic claims a proven speed limit for factoring that experts say leaves encryption untouched, DeepMind lets agents steer part of Gemini's experiment compute, Google tells agents to reach Gmail, Drive and Calendar through MCP by February, 42 attorneys general oppose Character.AI's bankruptcy auction, Anthropic's study of 58 firms finds review is the bottleneck, Tidal bans fully AI-made music, and diagram-design teaches agents to draw.

Viral / open-source spotlight

Diagram-design: a skill that makes coding agents draw clean, consistent diagrams

diagram-design (github.com/cathrynlavery/diagram-design) is an open-source skill, a folder of instructions and examples that a coding agent loads when a task calls for it. You describe a diagram in plain language, such as a system architecture, a flowchart, a timeline or a database layout, and the agent picks one of 52 diagram types, states its plan and writes a single web page with the drawing inside it. The file opens offline in any browser with no extra software, and can be exported as an image. The skill's value is its rules. It allows one accent colour used on one or two elements, three typefaces, thin borders, no shadows, and positions that all fall on a grid of four, so diagrams made on different days look like one set. It can redraw existing draw.io, Mermaid, Excalidraw and some PlantUML files in the same style, and can pick up a company's colours and fonts from its website. It installs into Claude Code as a plugin and works with Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor and others. The repository page showed about 73,100 stars and 4,900 forks when we read it, under the MIT licence, and one tracker counted 1,133 new stars on November 25. Why it is taking off: Agents write documents and plans all day, and their diagrams have been the weak part: cluttered, inconsistent and obviously machine-made. This skill shows that the fix is a tight set of design constraints and worked examples, not a bigger model. It is also another sign that skills, small packages of know-how such as Addy Osmani's agent-skills (Day 231), are how expertise is now shared between agent users. The caveats come from the project's own page: quality depends on the model, the same request can come out with a different layout each time, and the result is a finished picture, not an editable source, so the author recommends Mermaid for documents that live in a code repository and change often. Also trending: Alibaba's Open Code Review, which pairs fixed rule checks with an AI reviewer and trades some recall for fewer false alarms, and minimind (Day 239), which trains a 64-million-parameter language model from scratch in about two hours on one graphics card.

Part 1Google's Cogentic Posts Six AI-Written Maths Papers

On November 25 Google Research added six mathematics papers to its public GitHub repository, each attributed to Cogentic, a system in which several AI agents work together on a proof, according to press reports. Most reports say it runs on Gemini 4; one says Gemini 3.1 Pro with an early Gemini 4 model, and Google has not said which model produced these papers. The lead paper claims that any whole number can be split into its prime factors within a stated time limit that is proven outright, with no unproven assumptions. Other papers claim a speed-up for the discrete logarithm problem in certain number systems, a fast method for finding near-stable strategies in two-player games (within one fifth of a Nash equilibrium), and results on the log-rank conjecture and edge reconstruction. None has been peer reviewed. Cogentic's own paper is reported to say that domain experts checked each result, which is human review; the machine-checkable versions in the Lean proof language are promised for later and are not yet public. Computer scientist Scott Aaronson is quoted as saying the papers contain "nothing of practical relevance for cryptography". The concept, explained simply: A proven bound and a practical speed are different things. Much online encryption rests on the fact that multiplying two large primes is easy and undoing it, factoring, is slow. The fastest factoring method in use works well, but its speed estimate leans on assumptions nobody has proved. Think of two couriers. One nearly always delivers in two days but promises nothing. The other gives a written guarantee of delivery within 105 days. The guarantee is new and real, but no parcel arrives sooner. That is the reported result: commentators say the proven limit carries a constant of 105 where the practical method's estimate has about 1.9, and because that number sits in an exponent, the guaranteed method would be far slower at real key sizes. Encryption is no weaker today than it was on Tuesday. Why it matters: On Day 241 one AI-assisted proof passed a formal check after days of work by the Lean community. Now six papers arrive in a day with no machine check attached. AI can produce candidate mathematics faster than people or proof checkers can confirm it, so the scarce step is verification. Treat headlines about AI and encryption with care, and treat an unchecked proof as a claim, whoever or whatever wrote it.

Part 2DeepMind Lets Agents Steer Part of Gemini's Compute

Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development at Google DeepMind, said on the company's podcast that AI agents now control part of the computing power used to run experiments for the next Gemini model, according to The Decoder and outlets citing it. He also said the lab is still far from recursive self-improvement. He did not say what share of compute the agents control or which kinds of experiment they run. The same coverage says DeepMind deliberately leaves the agents' written reasoning, their chain of thought, out of training so that people can review it. Most reports date the remarks to this week; one says the episode came out on November 19.

The concept, explained simply: Recursive self-improvement means an AI that improves its own successor, which improves the next one, in a loop that no longer needs people. What is described here is narrower: automated experimentation. Picture a lab assistant who is allowed to book the equipment and run tests overnight. That is different from an assistant who redesigns the lab and hires their own replacement. People still set the goals and decide what ships. The second idea is keeping reasoning readable. A model's chain of thought is the working notes it writes before acting. If you grade those notes during training, the model can learn to write notes that look good instead of notes that show what it is doing. Leaving them ungraded keeps them a more honest window.

Why it matters: Compute is the scarcest resource inside an AI lab, so letting agents spend some of it is real delegation, not a demo. It also explains why controls such as OpenAI's 35-second off switch for research workloads (Day 229) are being built now. The questions to ask of any lab making this claim are how much the agents control, what limits apply and who can stop a run. For your own organisation the lesson is the same at small scale: give an agent a budget only with a cap, a log and a person who reads it.

Part 3Google Sets an MCP-Only Door for Workspace Agents

On November 24 Google made its Workspace MCP servers and an official command-line tool generally available, according to press and developer coverage. With them came a rule: from February 1, 2027, AI agents must reach Workspace data through these servers or the command-line tool, not through the general programming interfaces (REST APIs) that other software uses, and Google says it will enforce this technically. An agent must identify itself with a setting called is_agentic when it asks for access, and the MCP servers are reported to refuse clients that are not marked as agents. A free Standard tier and a paid Scaled tier apply first to Gmail, Drive and Calendar, with billing for the Scaled tier starting April 1, 2027. The concept, explained simply: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard plug that lets an AI application use outside tools. The new part is a separate, labelled entrance. Think of an office building where couriers must use the loading dock, sign in as couriers and have their visits logged, while staff use the front door. Both get in, but the building now knows which visitors are couriers, can limit what they carry and can charge for heavy use. Declaring agent identity is the sign-in step: software says it is an agent acting for a person, so an administrator can see, restrict or switch off agent access without touching ordinary apps. Why it matters: This is the first large platform we have seen make MCP mandatory for agents and not just available. It fits the pattern of websites locking out unlabelled agents (Day 230) and Walmart's Agent Gateway (Day 239): platforms want agents on a channel they can meter and govern. Any team with scripts or agents that read mail or files through Google's older interfaces should check before February 1 whether those count as agents. The open question is the definition, since the label is self-declared.

Part 4States Fight Character.AI's Bankruptcy Chat Auction

A bipartisan group of 42 state attorneys general has asked a bankruptcy court to reject Character.AI's planned sale of its user data, according to press reports. The companion-chatbot company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, and an auction is set for December 1. The states say the data covers chat histories from more than 21 million US accounts, more than 2.1 million of them belonging to minors, along with IP addresses and other metadata; reports add that profiles can carry risk scores the company gave to flagged users. The opening bidder, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, was formed one day before it was chosen and has not disclosed its funding. The states argue that a buyer would not be bound by Character.AI's privacy promises and that the company had told users their data would not be sold. California's attorney general said any sale must leave out children's chats and other sensitive data. The company has said it is not a data broker. We found no ruling yet. The concept, explained simply: When a company goes bankrupt, everything of value becomes an asset to be sold so that creditors are repaid, and customer data counts. A privacy policy is a promise made by the company. If the company is broken up, whether that promise travels with the data is for the court to decide. It is like a doctor's surgery that closes and sells its patient files along with the furniture: the new owner never made the patients any promise. Courts can attach conditions to such a sale or carve data out of it, which is what the states are asking for.

Why it matters: Conversations with a companion chatbot are among the most personal records a person creates, and here many belong to children. The wider point reaches every AI product. After the sell-off of Day 240, some AI vendors will fail or be bought, and what you typed into them is part of what gets sold. Before trusting a service with sensitive material, check what its terms say about a sale or insolvency, and delete what you can while the company still answers.

Part 5Anthropic's Study of 58 Firms Finds Review Is the Bottleneck

Anthropic published a report called Working with AI, based on 66 interviews across 58 US companies and covering nearly 300 uses of AI at work, according to press summaries. Interviewees said 55% of those uses raised output or quality, while 19% had delivered no business value so far. The obstacle mentioned most often was the volume of AI output that needs reviewing (49 mentions), ahead of employee resistance (43) and the need for expert review (42). Two thirds of the companies said they are hiring fewer people because of AI. Only two reported layoffs directly tied to AI, and five had dismissed workers who refused to use it. The companies were picked for variety and are not a representative sample, and the value ratings came from what interviewees said, not from measured tests. Anthropic also sells the tools in question.

The concept, explained simply: A process moves only as fast as its slowest step, which is called the bottleneck. Fit a kitchen with an oven twice as fast and the restaurant serves no more meals if there is still one waiter. AI makes drafts, code and analyses quickly, but someone must still check them, so the queue moves from making to checking. The firms that reported the most value were said to have reorganised the work around that fact, deciding what needs expert review and what does not, and not simply handing out tools. Why it matters: This is yesterday's Claude Ship story seen from the customer's side, and the same shape as today's maths papers: production is cheap and verification is scarce. It also refines the jobs picture from Day 228. The common effect in this sample is slower hiring, not layoffs, which is harder to see and falls on people who were never taken on. Read the percentages as testimony from a vendor's study, and measure your own use cases before quoting them.

Part 6Tidal Bans Fully AI-Generated Music

The music-streaming service Tidal said it will reject and remove tracks made wholly by AI from December 9, according to its own post as reported by the press. Tidal said that over the past 90 days 43% of all tracks delivered to it were detected as wholly AI-generated, and that about 27 million tracks in its catalogue carry that tag, 6.3% of everything on the service; some outlets give 29 million. Music that was made with help from AI but by a person stays allowed. Spotify and Apple Music label such tracks or keep them out of recommendations, but still accept them. The concept, explained simply: Streaming services mostly pay from a shared pot. Subscription money goes into one pool each month and is divided according to each track's share of all plays. So a flood of machine-made tracks does not need to be popular to matter: every play it gathers, sometimes from automated listeners, takes a slice that would have gone to working musicians. When making a track costs almost nothing, the service has to act as a filter. The filter is a detector, software that estimates whether audio was machine-made, and detectors make mistakes in both directions. Why it matters: Tidal is the first large music service we have seen ban this material where its bigger rivals label it. The same pressure applies wherever AI makes supply nearly free, including app stores, book shops and job applications. Two things deserve attention: how Tidal draws the line between generated and assisted, and how an artist who is wrongly flagged can appeal. A ban is only as fair as its error handling.

Market signal

The signal is that producing AI output is no longer the constraint, and the value is moving to whoever checks, labels and governs it. Google's agents produced six papers in a day and the world's mathematicians now have to verify them, while Anthropic's own customers name review as their main obstacle. Google is building a metered entrance for agents and will charge for heavy use from April, and Tidal is spending effort to keep machine-made supply out. A failed AI company's most valuable remaining asset turns out to be its users' private chats. One digest reports that Anthropic's shares closed below their $83 IPO price this week, and October reports put a second Nscale compute deal of about $45 billion in talks; we could confirm neither as of today. Expect platform owners to price agent access separately, more marketplaces to filter generated content, and buyers of AI services to ask what happens to their data if the vendor fails.

Practical takeaways
Separate a proven guarantee from a practical speed-up.

When a headline says AI cracked a hard problem, ask whether anything now runs faster in practice or whether a limit was proved on paper, and wait for an independent check either way.

Give agents a budget only with a cap, a log and an owner.

If agents may spend compute or money, set a hard limit, record every decision and name the person who reviews the record.

Keep an agent's reasoning readable.

Store the reasoning trace of important agent runs and do not reward or tune the agent on how those notes look, so they stay useful for oversight.

Check your Google Workspace integrations before February 1, 2027.

List every script, bot and agent that reads Gmail, Drive or Calendar, decide which count as agents, and plan their move to the MCP servers or the official command-line tool.

Ask every AI vendor what happens to your data if it is sold or fails.

Look for a clause on bankruptcy and acquisition, prefer services that let you delete history, and keep sensitive material out of those that do not.

Find your review bottleneck before buying more AI.

Measure how long AI output waits to be checked, and decide which kinds of work need an expert's eye and which can pass with a lighter test.

Plan for mistakes in any AI-content filter.

If you run or rely on a detector for generated content, define the line between generated and assisted and give people a way to appeal.

Give agents design rules, not just a request.

For diagrams and documents, a short list of constraints and a few good examples improves results more than a longer prompt.

Self-test
Why does Cogentic's reported factoring result not weaken encryption?

It proves a guaranteed time limit, but that limit is far slower than the methods already used in practice, so no key becomes easier to break.

What is the difference between automated experimentation and recursive self-improvement?

In the first, agents run tests that people direct and judge; in the second, an AI improves its own successors in a loop without people.

Why would a lab leave its agents' chain of thought out of training?

So the notes stay an honest record of what the agent is doing and are not shaped to look good to a grader.

What must an AI agent do to reach Gmail, Drive or Calendar from February 1, 2027?

Go through Google's Workspace MCP servers or official command-line tool and identify itself as an agent with the is_agentic setting.

Why can a bankrupt company's buyer be free of its privacy promises?

The policy was the old company's promise; user data is sold as an asset, and the promise follows only if the court makes it a condition of the sale.

In Anthropic's study, what obstacle was mentioned most often?

The volume of AI output that people have to review, with 49 mentions.

How do fully AI-generated tracks reduce what human musicians earn?

Royalties come from a shared pool split by share of plays, so every play of a generated track takes a slice from everyone else.

What we're watching

Outside mathematicians' first verdicts on the Cogentic papers, the promised Lean versions, and whether OpenAI or Anthropic publish AI-written mathematics of their own. What We're Watching: Any figure from DeepMind on how much compute its agents control, and other labs' statements on agent-run experiments. What We're Watching: Developers' reaction to Google's Workspace MCP rule, the prices of the Scaled tier, and whether Microsoft sets a similar rule for Microsoft 365. What We're Watching: The bankruptcy court's response to the 42 attorneys general before Character.AI's December 1 auction, and who bids. What We're Watching: Attribution of the breach of an unclassified CIA and ODNI system, where reports say investigators suspect the Artex AI hacking tool, and of the separate incident at the Treasury's FinCEN; also AWS re:Invent from November 30 and Black Friday data on agent-driven shopping.
