item.title: A Stolen Key Poisons a Coding-Agent Extension, Nine Nations Sign a Pact to Guard AI Supply Chains, and IBM and Microsoft Ship 6,000 Agents
item.dc:creator: Varun Singla
item.description: Cursor traces a trojanised Claude Code extension to a leaked Fireworks AI key, the US and eight partners sign the Pax Silica supply-chain accord, IBM and Microsoft launch Imagine Enterprise, Fractile raises $720 million…
item.content:encoded:
Cursor traces a trojanised Claude Code extension to a leaked Fireworks AI key, the US and eight partners sign the Pax Silica supply-chain accord, IBM and Microsoft launch Imagine Enterprise, Fractile raises $720 million for memory-first inference chips, and AiSOC is the open-source AI security centre developers are starring.

Viral / open-source spotlight

AiSOC: an open-source AI security operations centre

AiSOC (github.com/beenuar/AiSOC) is an MIT-licensed, self-hostable security operations centre in which AI agents investigate alerts. It ingests security telemetry, correlates related alerts into incidents, and lets agents research each one, but any response they propose (such as isolating a machine) must be approved by a human. Every prompt, tool call and line of reasoning is logged and can be replayed. It starts with a clone and 'make up' on Docker (one guide suggests 8 GB of free memory), and threat intelligence works without any API key by using CISA's public Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue. One report says the security firm Cyble funds the work; one tracker put it at about 5,500 stars in late October, and it has kept appearing on trending lists in November. Why it is taking off: Security teams are overwhelmed by alerts, and commercial 'AI SOC' products are expensive. AiSOC gives small teams a free, inspectable version they can run on their own hardware, so sensitive logs never leave the building. Its design also matches the safety patterns this series keeps returning to: agents propose, humans approve, and everything is replayable. It fits today's theme too, since an incident like Cursor's poisoned extension is exactly what a SOC must spot. Treat it as a lab tool first; check the code and test it on sample data before connecting production systems.

Part 1One Leaked Key Poisons Cursor's Claude Code Extension

Cursor disclosed on November 13 that a credential it had issued to Fireworks AI, the inference provider whose breach was covered on Day 228, was used to attack its extension marketplace. Attackers first copied data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor shared with Fireworks. Then, on October 29, they used a stolen credential to place trojanised copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in Cursor's marketplace cache. The bad build was live for about 11 hours and tried to plant an SSH key and set up background persistence on Windows and macOS. Cursor estimates that at most 5,000 users who requested the cached version may have received it. It deactivated the Fireworks key, rotated credentials, moved inference off Fireworks and rebuilt its marketplace. The concept, explained simply: This is a software supply-chain attack. Instead of hacking you directly, the attacker poisons something you trust and install automatically, here a coding-agent extension. The weak point was a cache: a local copy of popular packages kept for speed. If someone can write to the cache, every user who downloads from it gets their version, even though the original source (Open VSX, according to one report) was never infected. A coding-agent extension is a very valuable target because it runs with your permissions, can read your code and secrets, and can run shell commands.

Why it matters: Days 228-229 warned that AI platform credentials are the easiest way in; this is the follow-on harm, showing how one leaked partner key spread across companies. Coding-agent extensions now sit in the same risk class as browser extensions and npm packages. Expect signed extensions, pinned versions and per-partner, least-privilege keys to become the norm for AI developer tools.

Part 2Pax Silica: The US and Eight Partners Sign an AI Supply-Chain Pact

The Financial Times reported on November 15 that Japan, Australia, Israel, the UK, South Korea, India, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates signed an accord with the United States to protect AI supply chains, under a US-led initiative called Pax Silica. Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the European Commission were expected to sign the following week. The pact covers semiconductors, critical minerals, energy and industrial capacity, and sets up working groups to find weak points and build economic hubs. Reports say it does not create new export controls or chip-tracking rules and names no companies, and it comes ahead of a planned Trump-Xi meeting. The concept, explained simply: An AI supply chain is everything needed to build and run AI: rare minerals, chip factories, lithography machines, power plants and data centres. A pact like this is a 'friend-shoring' agreement: countries agree to source key parts from each other and plan together, so no single rival can cut off supply. It is a coordination framework, not a law; the details come later through working groups. Why it matters: Earlier issues covered the compute race, and Days 229-230 covered Google's specialised TPUs and Nvidia's leadership change. Pax Silica is the political layer underneath: where chips and power come from is now a matter of national security. For companies, it means AI infrastructure choices (which cloud region, which chip, which country) will increasingly carry geopolitical risk, and Gulf states are becoming central partners.

Part 3IBM and Microsoft Launch Imagine Enterprise with 6,000+ Agents and Assets

IBM and Microsoft announced Imagine Enterprise on November 10, a joint platform for building, deploying and governing AI agents in large companies. IBM Consulting contributes more than 6,000 prebuilt agents and assets; Microsoft supplies the technology through Microsoft Foundry, GitHub Copilot and Copilot Studio, plus its cloud, data and security services. The first industry frameworks target financial services, insurance and retail, and IBM forward-deployed engineers help clients set it up. Pricing, general availability and named production customers have not been disclosed, and the 6,000 figure counts agents and other assets together. In the same week Perplexity launched Teammates, persistent named agents for Max subscribers that keep their own memory and act on triggers from tools like Slack and GitHub.

The concept, explained simply: Think of an agent catalogue as an app store of ready-made workers: a claims-triage agent for an insurer, or a returns agent for a retailer, each pre-wired to common systems. A forward-deployed engineer is a vendor engineer who works inside the customer's company to fit those parts to real data and processes. The hard part of enterprise agents is rarely the model; it is connecting to old systems, permissions and audit, which is what consultants sell.

Why it matters: Earlier issues covered enterprise agent platforms; this deal shows the market dividing between labs that sell models and integrators that sell finished, governed agents. When evaluating such offers, ask how many of the 6,000 items are actually deployable agents, which run in production today, and who owns the logs and kill switch (Day 232). Persistent agents like Teammates show the same direction for smaller teams.

Part 4Fractile Raises $720 Million to Attack the Memory Wall

London-based Fractile raised a $720 million Series C at a reported $7 billion post-money valuation, according to Reuters and others, led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint, with backing from the UK's Sovereign AI Fund. That is roughly six times its valuation from the $220 million Series B in May. Anthropic reportedly signed an initial deal in August to buy about $250 million of Fractile's inference chips. Its first commercial chip is not due until 2027, and no independently verified performance numbers have been published. The concept, explained simply: When a model answers a question, most of the time is spent not calculating but moving model weights from memory to the processor. This bottleneck is called the memory wall. GPUs keep weights in separate DRAM chips and fetch them over a bus, which is like a chef walking to a distant pantry for every ingredient. Fractile puts the maths units right next to fast on-chip memory (SRAM) on the same die, so the ingredients are on the counter. The trade-off: SRAM is small and expensive, so very large models must be split across many chips. Why it matters: Inference, not training, is becoming the largest AI cost as agents run around the clock. A big valuation before any chip ships shows how badly labs want alternatives to Nvidia and to scarce, expensive high-bandwidth memory. For buyers, the lesson is to compare cost per token and latency on your own workload, not headline speed claims.

Market signal

Capital is pricing in AI as strategic infrastructure. Fractile's $7 billion valuation before a single chip ships, a government fund in its round, and a nine-nation pact on chips, minerals and power all point the same way: compute supply is now treated like energy security. Meanwhile, the Cursor incident shows the hidden cost side: every partner key and extension cache is a liability that can spread across companies. Anthropic's IPO, reported as heavily oversubscribed at its $70-$78 range, is expected to price around November 18 and begin Nasdaq trading as ANT around November 19 (press reports, not confirmed by the company). The signal: investors reward owners of scarce compute and trusted distribution, while security failures in the AI toolchain are becoming a material business risk.

Practical takeaways
Treat agent extensions like code you ship.

Pin versions, prefer signed extensions and review what your coding agent's plugins can run on your machine.

Give each partner its own narrow key.

Issue a separate, least-privilege, rotatable credential to every vendor so one leak cannot reach your other systems.

Check your machine after an extension scare.

Look for unknown SSH keys in authorized_keys and new startup items, then rotate any secrets the IDE could read.

Map where your AI compute comes from.

List the cloud regions, chips and countries your AI workloads depend on and note any single points of geopolitical risk.

Question agent-catalogue numbers.

Ask vendors how many catalogue items are deployable agents, which run in production, and who controls logs and shutdown.

Benchmark cost per token on your own workload.

Compare new inference hardware or providers by cost and latency on your real prompts, not by headline speed claims.

Try an AI SOC in a sandbox.

Run AiSOC on sample logs to see how agent-led triage with human approval could fit your security process.

Self-test
How did attackers deliver a malicious Claude Code extension to Cursor users?

They used a stolen credential linked to the Fireworks AI breach to place trojanised copies in Cursor's marketplace cache, which served them for about 11 hours.

What is a software supply-chain attack?

An attack that poisons something users trust and install automatically, such as a package, extension or update, instead of attacking each user directly.

What does the Pax Silica accord cover?

Coordinated protection of AI supply chains: semiconductors, critical minerals, energy and industrial capacity, through working groups rather than new export controls.

What is the memory wall, and how does Fractile try to beat it?

Inference is slowed by moving weights from off-chip DRAM to the processor; Fractile places compute next to on-chip SRAM on the same die.

Why does AiSOC require human approval for responses?

Its agents only propose actions such as isolating a machine; a person approves them, and every step is logged and replayable.

What we're watching

What We're Watching: whether Cursor publishes a full post-mortem and whether other AI tools find similar cache or partner-key exposure. What We're Watching: Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the European Commission signing Pax Silica, and any official text from the State Department. What We're Watching: Anthropic's IPO pricing around November 18 and its first day of trading as ANT. What We're Watching: the first named production customers and pricing for IBM and Microsoft's Imagine Enterprise. What We're Watching: independent benchmarks of Fractile's chip and whether other labs follow Anthropic as customers.

Sources. bleepingcomputer.com, thehackernews.com, securityonline.info and dev.to (Cursor / Fireworks extension incident); bloomberg.com and seekingalpha.com (citing the Financial Times), thenews.com.pk, polandinsight.com and mlq.ai (Pax Silica); ciodive.com, analyticsindiamag.com and runtimewire.com (Imagine Enterprise); techrepublic.com and letsdatascience.com (Perplexity Teammates); siliconangle.com, thenextweb.com, tomshardware.com and runtimewire.com (Fractile); github.com/beenuar/AiSOC, beenuar.github.io/AiSOC and explainx.ai (AiSOC). Figures are secondary reports and unverified unless from the company's own page or filing.

item.title: Agents Get a Wallet, Security Firms Build Agent Kill Switches, and Cloudflare Opens a Browser Made for Bots
item.dc:creator: Varun Singla
item.description: OpenAI's ChatGPT Wallet lets its dots agents pay with tokenised cards and a biometric check, CrowdStrike adds an AI Kill Switch while security vendors race to buy agent-identity startups, Thinking Machines opens the…
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI's ChatGPT Wallet lets its dots agents pay with tokenised cards and a biometric check, CrowdStrike adds an AI Kill Switch while security vendors race to buy agent-identity startups, Thinking Machines opens the weights of its 594-billion-parameter Inkling 2 Small, and Cloudflare open-sources Kitesurf, a lightweight browser engine for AI agents.

Viral / open-source spotlight

Cloudflare Kitesurf: a browser engine built for AI agents

Cloudflare open-sourced Kitesurf under Apache 2.0 (changelog dated November 12, blog November 13). It is an experimental browser engine written in Rust and WebAssembly that loads pages, runs JavaScript and renders layouts without needing Chromium or a full browser container. It combines Blitz for HTML, DOM and layout, Stylo (Firefox's CSS engine) for styling and Boa for JavaScript. Clients connect over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, so existing Puppeteer scripts work without rewrites, and developers can run it locally or deploy it to their own Cloudflare account. Extensions are deliberately left out, the hosted Browser Run service is not part of the release, and Cloudflare says it is under heavy development. Why it is taking off: Browsing is the most expensive part of many agents: each Chromium instance eats hundreds of megabytes, which limits how many agents a company can run at once. A lighter engine that speaks the same protocol as Chrome means cheaper, faster agent browsing with no code changes, and the release was picked up widely by developer outlets. One report claims about seven times less memory on typical agent tasks, not confirmed by Cloudflare. It also fits the day's theme: Cloudflare sits between websites and bots, so it is shaping both how agents browse and how sites decide whether to let them in. Expect sites that break without full Chromium, so test before switching.

Part 1ChatGPT Wallet: OpenAI's Agents Can Now Pay

OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on November 13. It lets dots, the always-on proactive agents covered on Day 223, complete purchases for the user. The first rollout is narrow: US ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and over with eligible US-issued cards, and only inside dots conversations, not ordinary chats or ChatGPT Work. Visa, Mastercard and American Express are the main partners. The agent never sees the real card: payments use network tokens, full card numbers and CVVs are not stored, and every purchase must be approved with Face ID, Touch ID or a similar biometric check. OpenAI takes no commission for now, warns that agents can make mistakes, and notes that merchants and card issuers can still decline. It says users will later be able to pre-approve purchases within limits such as spending caps, categories or time windows. The concept, explained simply: A payment token is a stand-in card number that only works for one merchant, device or purpose. If it leaks, the thief cannot reuse it elsewhere, and it can be cancelled without replacing your real card. The biometric check is a 'human in the loop' step: the agent fills the basket and prepares the payment, but money moves only when the person physically confirms. Pre-approved limits ('up to $50 on groceries this week') are the next step, a budget the agent may spend without asking each time. Why it matters: This is the first big consumer test of agents spending money, and it copies the guardrail pattern seen in Anthropic's read-only finance feature (Day 224): narrow access, tokens instead of secrets, and explicit approval. It also collides with the lockout story from Days 230-231: Amazon and United block third-party agents, so a wallet only helps where merchants agree to let agents in. Expect card networks, not AI labs, to become the gatekeepers of agentic commerce.

Part 2CrowdStrike's AI Kill Switch: Containing Agents That Misbehave

At Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona, CrowdStrike unveiled an AI Kill Switch in its Falcon Guardian product. Administrators can stop a misbehaving agent, block it from relaunching on chosen machines and cut its network access, with every action logged. The first working mechanism is at the gateway: Falcon Guardian tells connected AI gateways (CrowdStrike's own Falcon AI Gateway, included at no extra cost, or a third-party one) to block the agent's access to the models it calls. Reports disagree on whether stopping agents directly on the endpoint is live or still coming soon, and SaaS-hosted agents are covered through Falcon Shield. CrowdStrike also agreed to buy Fiddler (AI observability) and Dreadnode (AI red-teaming) for a combined $495 million, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The concept, explained simply: An AI gateway is a checkpoint that every request from an agent to a model passes through, like a building's single front door. If you control the door, you can stop an agent instantly without finding every copy of it, because an agent that cannot reach its model can no longer think or act. Killing the process on the laptop or server is the second line, for agents that run local models or have already started a harmful action. Why it matters: Day 229 covered OpenAI's 35-second Control Room for its own research workloads; this is the same idea sold to ordinary companies. The gateway design only works if all agent traffic is forced through it, so the real lesson is architectural: route every agent's model calls through one place you can switch off, and check vendor claims about endpoint termination before relying on them.

Part 3Thinking Machines Opens Inkling 2 Small's 594B Weights

Thinking Machines Lab, Mira Murati's startup, launched Inkling 2 Small on November 5 as a hosted-only model on its Tinker platform, then posted the weights on Hugging Face on November 12 under Apache 2.0, crediting its team and safety-testing partners. It is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 594 billion total parameters but only 17 billion active per token, accepts images and has a 1-million-token context window. Two repositories are listed: a main NVFP4 checkpoint (about 394 GB, needing at least 500 GB of combined GPU memory) and an MXFP8 version (about 623 GB, at least 800 GB). Artificial Analysis ranks it fourth of 28 open-weight models with an Intelligence Index of 31, and one review notes DeepSeek V4.1 Flash leads on most coding rows of the lab's own model card.

The concept, explained simply: 'Small' here means small for the lab, not small for your laptop. In a mixture-of-experts model, each word is sent to only a few specialist sub-networks, so it computes like a 17B model but must store all 594B parameters in memory. NVFP4 and MXFP8 are low-precision number formats (4-bit and 8-bit) that shrink each stored parameter; fewer bits means less memory and faster maths, at a small cost in accuracy. The 'closed first, open a week later' pattern gives a lab time to watch for misuse before anyone can download and modify the model.

Why it matters: Another strong Apache-licensed model widens the open-weight field after Kimi K3.1 Pro (Day 223), giving firms a model they can host privately for data-sensitive work. But the hardware bill (a multi-GPU server) means most teams will use it through hosted providers, and the staged release is becoming a template that balances openness with a safety check.

Part 4The Agent-Identity Buying Spree

Security vendors are paying high prices for startups that manage what AI agents are allowed to access. Palo Alto Networks is reported (first by The Information, then TechCrunch) to be in talks to buy Clutch Security for about $500 million in cash plus milestone payments; Clutch is said to be nearing $10 million in annual recurring revenue, about 50 times revenue and roughly six times its last $85 million valuation. No deal is signed, and neither company commented. It would be Palo Alto's seventh acquisition this year. Reports also cite Cyera completing a roughly $1 billion purchase of Oasis Security and Cisco buying Astrix for about $400 million, plus CrowdStrike's $495 million pair.

The concept, explained simply: Every agent needs credentials (API keys, tokens, service accounts) to touch email, code or databases. These are 'non-human identities', and in many companies they already outnumber employees. Agent-identity tools keep an inventory of them, give each only the permissions it needs, rotate secrets and flag an agent that suddenly reaches for something new, much as HR and IT manage staff badges. Why it matters: Days 228-229 showed that stolen credentials on AI platforms are the easiest way in. Buyers paying 50 times revenue are betting that agent identity becomes a standard budget line like antivirus. For teams, the practical question is simple: can you list every agent key you have issued, and revoke one in minutes?

Market signal

Money is flowing to the control layer around agents. Card networks are lending their tokens to ChatGPT Wallet, CrowdStrike is spending $495 million and Palo Alto may spend $500 million on agent safety and identity, and Cloudflare is giving away the browser layer to sell the network underneath.

Practical takeaways
Never give an agent your real card.

Use tokenised wallets with per-purchase approval, and set low spending caps when pre-approval arrives.

Route every agent through one gateway.

Send all agent model calls through a single AI gateway so you can block an agent in one step.

Rehearse your kill switch.

Test stopping, blocking relaunch and cutting network access for one agent before you need it in an incident.

Inventory your non-human identities.

List every API key and service account used by agents, give each least privilege and practise revoking one.

Check memory before you pick an open model.

Inkling 2 Small computes like 17B but needs 500 GB of GPU memory; use a host unless you have the hardware.

Try a lighter agent browser in a sandbox.

Point a Puppeteer test suite at Kitesurf and compare memory, speed and page breakage against Chromium.

Self-test
What protects the user's card when a dots agent pays through ChatGPT Wallet?

A network token stands in for the real card number, card details are not stored, and each purchase needs biometric approval.

How does CrowdStrike's AI Kill Switch stop an agent today?

It tells connected AI gateways to block the agent's access to its models, and can also block relaunch and network access, with logging.

Why can a 594B mixture-of-experts model run like a 17B one but still need huge memory?

Only about 17B parameters are active per token, but all 594B must be stored and loaded.

What is a non-human identity?

A credential such as an API key, token or service account used by software or an AI agent rather than a person.

Why can existing Puppeteer scripts drive Cloudflare Kitesurf?

Kitesurf speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol, the same interface Puppeteer uses to control Chrome.

What we're watching

independent tests of ChatGPT Wallet: which merchants accept dots agents and how often purchases fail. What We're Watching: whether CrowdStrike confirms endpoint-level agent termination as live, and how rivals respond. What We're Watching: whether Palo Alto Networks signs the Clutch Security deal. What We're Watching: Anthropic's IPO pricing around November 18 and whether it lands above the $70-$78 range. What We're Watching: community benchmarks of Kitesurf against Chromium and early fine-tunes of Inkling 2 Small.
